text: Why do we see three dots instantly, but have to guess when there are eight? Our new paper in eye-Perception proposes an answer: the numbers we know work like the valleys of a landscape.
A quick experiment. Some dots will flash on the screen. Don’t count them: just say how many you see.
With three, the answer was just there. With eight, you had to estimate.
Everyone shows this pattern. Up to three or four, we are almost always right, and fast. Beyond that, each extra dot makes us less accurate and slower.

The usual explanation is two systems. For small sets, an object tracking system follows up to about four items at once, exactly. For large sets, an approximate number system gives an estimate that gets noisier as numbers grow.
But in between, the curve falls smoothly, with no jump, and neither system really captures that transition. So where would the border be?

To find an answer, we borrowed an idea from the science of memory. In nineteen eighty-two, the physicist John Hopfield proposed a network of artificial neurons that stores memories and recovers them from incomplete or noisy versions. This work earned him a share of the twenty twenty-four Nobel Prize in Physics.
A Hopfield network can be pictured as a landscape, where each memory is a valley.
When a song starts, its first notes drop a ball somewhere on this landscape.
As the song goes on, the network relaxes: the ball rolls downhill until it settles at the bottom of a valley. That is the moment you recognise the song.
Some memories are deeper than others.
With a song you know very well, the valley is deep, and the relaxation is very fast.
With a song you barely know, the valley is wide and shallow. The relaxation is slow, and the ball may even end up in a similar song.
Now swap songs for numbers. Here the Hopfield landscape is special: it has a single dimension.

The valleys sit in a row, so the relations between them matter: neighbouring valleys are neighbouring numbers. This row is our mental number line, and it tells us which numbers are larger than others.
Each number is a valley. Small numbers, which we meet all the time, get deep, narrow valleys. Larger numbers get wider ones.
The dots drop the ball, never quite in the right place.
Three lands near a steep valley and settles at once. Eight lands on an almost flat plain. The ball barely moves, so the answer could be seven, eight or nine, and it comes more slowly.
Repeat this many times, and the pattern we saw in people appears.
One landscape gives exact answers for small numbers and approximate ones for large numbers. No second system, and no border: the valleys simply widen.
We tested the model on almost fifty-three thousand answers from three hundred and seventy-nine adults. It captures which number people give, how often they are exactly right, and how long they take.
And it explains the answers better than the alternatives, including the classic approximate system.
Each person also has their own landscape. People whose valleys stay separate for longer are more precise when they estimate large quantities.
If numbers are memories, experience shapes their valleys. Counting, comparing and estimating quantities may be how we sculpt this landscape.
